chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: Entertainment versus pure jazz and singing the lyric
summary: She sees herself as an entertainer, comparing with instrumentalists who imitate voices, noting Lester Young knowing the words first.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: For them it's a new experience. So far as I'm concerned I do believe that there is going to be at least two generations inbetween the Swing era and what is currently popular. And it's a continuation of the Swing era. And getting back to what I said a long time ago, I do feel that the war nipped the Swing era in the bud. It did not have its chance to really evolve into what is next. You had swing, voomph, and then you had bop. I think music does have a sort of tendancy to link itself up a little bit. So here we are. We are going to finish it out. Of course jazz has always had a way of going underground for different reasons or other and when the early jazz you didn't have all the outlets.

And of course jazz I think you have to say that you have to be exposed to it. Jazz as we know it is more or less dancible, and if you can give the beat and give the swing music then you can play Swing and jazz and be alright. The current music, what they call the eclectic music, it's for the players and maybe a sort of discriminating audience who digs seriously, takes music seriously, that understand it and enjoy it. But there are allot of people out there that are not that involved in music. They just want to be entertained and they want to dance and they want to have fun. They don't want to have to figure out what the guys are doing. And of course if you're not a highly educated musician you don't understand when these guys go on these extensions of harmonies and things like that. And even though I might understand it I can't listen to that all the time. I mean, I want to relax too.
Is that the audience you've defined for yourself? I mean, people want to be entertained rather than, let's say, you know, people who define singing as an art. I think jazz singing is an art form.

tainment. I remember some critic made a remark, one of the reasons why the musicians weren't getting the appreciation or the interest that they thought they should have got is because there is no showmanship there. And of course they were making a comparison. This was when business was bad and they couldn't figure out why. But Cab Calloway was pulling along strongly because Cab was a showman. So you have to - all the bands always had to do more than just play. Years ago I remember Ozzie Nelson, the band leader, and when they had bands on the stage and in his first number he would go out and stand on his head because he said he knew that's what he'd have to do before he got through. So you have to entertain the audience. And also I like to feel that there's a certain amount of communication that goes on between the performer and the audience. Being a singer and I don't know how this is with the musicians, but I happen to be in the position to deliver a lyric and I try to communicate through the lyrics of the song. And I feel that musicians have a way of communicating too. And when you take jazz musicians and they don't just play music, what can I say, when the tenor sax., for instance, he's

imitating a voice. He's not being articulate so far as lyric is concerned but he's saying something.
Well Lester Young always used to say he would never play a song unless he knew the words first.

That's right, you see what I mean? That's it. So I think that that's what you need to do. And if you're up there just playing all over your horn and showing how great you are, this does not necessarily say you're communicating. You're communicating, yeah, you're showing how fast you can move your fingers and how fast you can go. You know, it's kind of hard to figure out but if you watch . . .

Okay, I understand what you're saying about instrumental music. Now with singers what's the danger? Is there a comparible danger for singers that they lose contact with the people they're trying to entertain by let's saying, being too dazzling in their technique?
Yeah, well it shows it's a novelty. But, alright look at the singers today or singing groups for instance. Of course you got television

and that's a sight thing. You can't just stand up there and sing. You got to do something. Now a days they dance, they go into a whole act, and do their thing. You got more, there's more of a media, there's more of an outlet with all kinds of talent now. On television you have to do something besides stand there and sing. You are an act so to speak. And if they take long shots, you know, what do you do with your hand, or what do you do with your feet? I think that's one of the reasons why we don't have as much exposure of jazz on TV because there definitely needs to be a little bit more action. I remember watching Arthur Fiedler's Christmas Show a couple of years ago and they were doing a medley of Christmas Songs, the Jingles, and the musicians were actually doing funny things like putting up umbrellas with the snow coming down, and on some of the little incidential notes they had to hit they were being kind of funny. They were - this was showmanship or otherwise you think of a big orchestra like that, stiff and blowing away and playing that music, but they were having fun and I think this is what we need to do.
